title: Is fluoride making us stupid?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine fluoride in drinking water and consumer products, covering its adoption in Grand Rapids, Michigan, the dental caries rationale, EPA limits of four parts per million, and dental and skeletal fluorosis. They then recount a conspiracy narrative linking fluoridation to aluminum, chemical and fertilizer industries, I.G. Farben, the revolving door (Oscar Ewing), Edward Bernays' PR campaigns, Manhattan Project redactions, the 2003 Water Act, and the firing of toxicologist Phyllis Mella Mullenix. They note that pharmaceutical-grade sodium fluoride was used in the old safety studies while cities often use hydrofluorosilicic acid, a byproduct of industrial processes. The episode closes with an EPA union scientist's opposition, a Hardy Limeback reference, listener mail about a ball lightning story, and a request for iTunes reviews.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to fluoride
segments.summary: Hosts introduce fluoride in water, toothpaste and other products, and note that many countries do not fluoridate while the US does.

segments.title: Origins of fluoridation and dental caries
segments.summary: Grand Rapids, Michigan became the first city to fluoridate water after scientists linked naturally fluoridated water to lower dental caries. The American Dental Association endorsed fluoride in 1969.

segments.title: Fluoride dangers and EPA limits
segments.summary: The EPA's optimal level is four parts per million, with levels up to fourteen considered dangerous. Risks discussed include dental and skeletal fluorosis, seizures, GI upset, and a correlation between high exposure and lower IQ, with studies from China.

segments.title: Industrial origins and the fluoride conspiracy
segments.summary: The hosts trace I.G. Farben's ties with Henry Ford, Standard Oil and Alcoa, and the fluoride cartel. They describe a claim that German chemists fluoridated prisoner-of-war water to make them docile, and Gerald Cox's rat study on cavities.

segments.title: Revolving door, PR and suppressed research
segments.summary: Oscar Ewing, a former Alcoa attorney, headed the Federal Security Agency and cities began fluoridating soon after. Edward Bernays' PR tactics are discussed, along with redacted Manhattan Project fluoride findings, the 2003 Water Act, and the firing of Phyllis Mullenix before her fluoride and ADHD findings were published.

segments.title: Pharmaceutical-grade sodium fluoride and hydrofluorosilicic acid
segments.summary: Hosts argue that safety studies used pharmaceutical-grade sodium fluoride, whereas many cities use hydrofluorosilicic acid, a industrial byproduct scrubbed from smokestacks. They cite EPA union scientist William Hirzy and Hardy Limeback as critics.

segments.title: Listener mail on ball lightning
segments.summary: Listeners respond to an earlier lightning-through-a-kitchen story, with a grad student noting it resembles ball lightning. The hosts also ask listeners to leave iTunes reviews.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the contact email and website and close the episode.
